Tunnel Hill – Vienna, Illinois
100 Mile

JPMorgan Chase & Co. said some transactions are taking longer to process than normal as the bank grapples with a “technical issue.”
Customers still have access to their accounts and funds, the bank said in an emailed statement Monday. The firm is working to resolve it as quickly as possible, according to the statement.
The disruption isn’t tied to a cybersecurity issue, according to a person familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified citing confidential details.
Tech challenges have been plaguing US companies and entities in recent weeks. Microsoft Corp. faced one of its longest outages last week, with disruptions to Outlook, Teams and the Copilot artificial intelligence tool. US airlines were hit by one of the longest nationwide shutdowns in decades, with the Federal Aviation Administration saying the ground stop was tied to a router located near El Dorado, Arkansas.
Downdetector had logged more than 3,000 reports of disruption Monday with JPMorgan. Other financial firms also saw a spike in reported disruptions including Bank of America Corp. and Wells Fargo & Co. Zelle, the payments system overseen by Early Warning Services and owned by banks, was also among the apps listed as customers flagged problems.
A representative for Bank of America declined to comment, while a Wells Fargo spokesperson had no immediate comment. A Zelle spokesperson said its system isn’t down and is operating as it should.
JPMorgan shares fell 2.6% to $337.26 at 2:45 p.m. in New York, narrowing this year’s gain to 4.7%. Bank of America was down 2.4%, while Wells Fargo dropped 2.2%.
Spokespeople for the Federal Reserve, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has dropped a lawsuit that accused the NCAA of misleading college sports fans by allowing transgender athletes to participate in events marketed as women’s competitions.
The lawsuit, filed in December 2024, said the NCAA falsely marketed events as women’s athletics in violation of the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act.
“Radical ‘gender theory’ has no place in college sports,” Paxton said in a 2024 news release announcing the lawsuit.
The attorney general’s office Thursday informed the state district court in Lubbock that it will not proceed with the lawsuit. The court filing was first reported by Bloomberg Law.
In a statement after the lawsuit was filed, the NCAA did not address the allegations but said it would continue to support women’s sports.
The attorney general’s office and the NCAA did not immediately respond to requests for comment Friday.
Paxton’s office has dropped at least two other lawsuits since the Nov. 3 election when Paxton lost his bid for the U.S. Senate and Democrat Nathan Johnson defeated Republican Mayes Middleton to become the next attorney general. Johnson has said he intends to review Paxton-era lawsuits and halt action on those deemed political in nature.
Last week, Paxton’s office dropped a lawsuit seeking to shut down FIEL, a Houston immigrant-rights organization the state had accused of violating nonprofit restrictions by criticizing the immigration policies of President Donald Trump and Gov. Greg Abbott.
Paxton’s office cited social media posts encouraging people to vote against Trump’s immigration proposals. The group opposed a 2023 Texas law that let Texas police arrest people suspected of having entered the country illegally.
The office also dropped a lawsuit seeking to shut down Annunciation House, an El Paso migrant shelter that Paxton accused of illegally harboring undocumented immigrants.
“It’s very gratifying that this has now ended. It’s over,” Ruben Garcia, founder and executive director of Annunciation House, told El Paso Matters.
Republican messaging during the midterm elections was sharply focused on transgender people, particularly regarding youth and sports. It was also a topic that Johnson and Middleton frequently clashed over on the campaign trail and dates back to their days in the Texas senate together.
Johnson singled out the 2025 “bathroom bill,” penned by Middleton, as one he would not devote resources to enforcing as attorney general.

The Kentucky Department of Insurance has approved a recommendation that will keep average workers’ compensation loss costs unchanged—a rare non-decrease in an era that has seen annual reductions in most states for the last two decades.
The 0.0% change for the voluntary market will take effect Jan. 1, the DOI said in a bulletin. It follows a 9.7% average decrease for 2026 and similar cuts in preceding years.
The National Council on Compensation Insurance in September recommended keeping the course on average loss costs for 2027, based on loss experience in Kentucky from policy years 2022, 2023 and 2024.
“Policy year 2024 produced a higher loss ratio than observed in the prior two policy years. It is not yet clear whether the loss ratio increase in policy year 2024 can be attributed to year-over-year volatility or the start of a longer-term trend in Kentucky,” the NCCI wrote in a summary of its recommendations.
The year 2024 saw an increase in claim frequency, a deviation from a historical pattern of declines in frequency, the NCCI noted. Indemnity claim severity remained stable, while medical severity decreased that year.
Across the 38 states for which NCCI serves as a rating and analytics agency, the 2025 combined ratio for workers’ comp insurers rose, from 86% to 91%. After many years of declining worker injury rates across the country, the Council said the change in combined ratio is due primarily to an increase in loss and underwriting expense ratios.
Payroll also has increased around the country, putting upward pressure on premiums.
“From 2024 to 2025, payroll increased 4.8%, while employment rose just 0.5%,” the NCCI noted. A significant portion of payroll growth appears to have come from higher wages, which were up an average of 4.3% in 2025. Employment growth was largely driven by the health care sector.

Global cyber insured losses from the Microsoft 365 outage on Nov. 12-14 are estimated by various industry observers to range from $100 million to $700 million.
CyberCube, the cyber risk analytics provider, estimates that the outage will most likely be less than $100 million, with a conservative upper limit estimated at $350 million.

Credit ratings agency Morningstar DBRS said: “In our view, the overall credit impact of the Microsoft outage on insurers is likely to be limited, with global insured losses estimates at US$300 million to US$500 million….”
Insurance broker Acrisure had a higher insurance loss estimate of US$700 million.
“Overall, the impact on the insurance market is expected to be minimal, with most losses likely limited to short-term productivity and operational delays,” said Marsh Re in a report titled “Delivery failed: Microsoft 365 outage.”
“Claims may nevertheless arise where policyholders relied on Microsoft 365 for critical, time-sensitive, or revenue-generating activities and the applicable waiting period was exceeded,” Marsh Re added. “The event also highlights the systemic and accumulation risks associated with reliance on a dominant technology provider, even where individual claims remain limited.”
Technical Issue, Not Cyber Activity
Microsoft attributed the outage to a technical issue introduced during a network capacity upgrade, not cyber activity, CyberCube said, explaining that severe disruption lasted about 18 hours, and the event ran roughly 38 hours in total – well beyond the eight to 12 hour waiting periods common in contingent system failure cover.
Despite the duration of the outage, CyberCube expects several factors will suppress insured losses.
“Cover only responds where policies extend business interruption to non-malicious system failure at an outside provider. Impacts reported from the event all focus on the inconvenience and productivity loss, with workarounds widely available and little to no mention of lost revenue,” the company said. “Simply put, email is not in the critical transaction path of most businesses.”
As of Nov. 13, Marsh Re described the outage as “a significant but uneven disruption with broad geographic exposure and progressive recovery,” but not a complete Microsoft 365 outage, a cloud infrastructure failure, nor or a cyberattack.
“Given that the disruption has exceeded 12 hours, potential business interruption or contingent business interruption losses may be relevant where insureds relied on Microsoft 365 for critical, time-sensitive, or revenue-generating operations,” Marsh Re said. “Overall, however, the impact on the insurance market is expected to be minimal, given the uneven nature of the disruption and likelihood that most losses will be limited to short-term productivity and operational delays.”

New World screwworm spreading rapidly across Southern states
A pinned specimen of a full-grown New World screwworm fly is shown in this image. Federal and state officials are grappling with a worsening infestation from the flesh-eating parasite that threatens livestock, pets and wildlife. (Photo courtesy of Michael Miller/Texas A&M AgriLife)
A deadly flesh-eating parasite that can plague livestock, wildlife and pets continues to spread across the American Southwest.
Officials detected the arrival of the New World screwworm in June — the first time in decades the pest had been seen in the United States. Since then, detections have spiked, with 139 recorded cases across three states. While fewer than 10 total cases were recorded in August and September, the U.S. Department of Agriculture has already confirmed 53 cases this month.
“We got a bunch more cases all of a sudden,” said David Anderson, professor and extension economist in livestock and food product marketing at Texas A&M University.
Rising infections have pushed state leaders to designate certain outbreak areas across Texas, New Mexico and Arizona, where animal movement is being restricted.
The movement of pets and livestock is restricted in all or parts of 31 Texas counties as officials there are tracking 77 sites with at least one confirmed case.
Contrary to its name, the screwworm grows into an adult fly about the size of a common housefly. The name screwworm refers to the larvae (maggots) that burrow into open wounds, feeding as they go “like a screw being driven into wood,” according to USDA.
The pest could threaten beef and dairy cattle — potentially exacerbating high prices for consumers. But the screwworm can also infect people, wildlife and pets. That’s pushed states to recommend or require certain monitoring of pet movements.
California, for instance, requires all warm-blooded animals coming from an infested zone to have a pretravel inspection, a veterinary certification and an entry permit into the state. In Texas, adoptions for thousands of dogs and cats were put on hold in August as most states restricted movement of animals from areas with screwworm infestations.
“It’s thrown a wrench into things, for small rescues as well as the bigger shelters,” Mia Bendixsen, executive director of the Texas Humane Legislation Network, told The Associated Press.
Earlier this month, the New Mexico Livestock Board broadened its screwworm tracking to regional infestation zones as more cases were confirmed across southern parts of the state. Those zones demarcate where ranchers must receive state authorization before moving cattle.
“We are working closely with our state and federal partners to investigate these cases, increase surveillance and monitor for additional infestations,” New Mexico State Veterinarian Samantha Holeck said in an October statement, according to Source New Mexico.
Screwworm maggots burrow into the flesh of living animals through wounds as small as a tick bite or in body openings such as the eyes or nose. That means ranchers must keep close watch over newborn calves with exposed umbilical cords and may need to rethink branding and tagging operations that provide an entry for the pests.
While the flies could prove deadly to herds, USDA says they do not create food safety risks.
But a worsening infestation could impact beef prices, which are already near record high prices.

Missouri Democrats rode an election wave. Could it carry them to power in 2028?
Democrats gained ground in virtually every corner of Missouri, opening a possible path to a House majority. Winning the Senate or a statewide office is a much steeper climb.
After sweeping gains in 2026, Missouri Democrats see a path to a House majority in 2028. But winning statewide or taking the Senate remains difficult (Jim Neuger/Maine Morning Star).
Scott Miller appears to have won another term in the Missouri House. Barely.
The St. Charles County Republican beat Democrat Chris Chapman by 67 votes on Nov. 3, according to unofficial results. It was a rematch. Two years ago, Miller beat Chapman by 3,288 votes. This time, the margin is close enough to qualify for a recount under state law.
Democrats flipped 16 House seats and broke the GOP’s supermajorities. Districts like Miller’s, where Republicans held on, may matter more for 2028.
In all 96 House districts where both parties fielded candidates in both 2024 and 2026, Democrats improved their share of the two-party vote. The average gain was nearly nine percentage points. And the shift extended deep into rural, Republican Missouri.
The auditor’s race provides another way to measure the shift because Republican Scott Fitzpatrick was on the ballot in both 2022 and 2026. The Democratic share of the two-party vote rose from 38.8% to 47.7%. The largest shifts came in Pemiscot County in the Bootheel, Jasper County around Joplin, and Clay and Cass counties in the Kansas City area.
Rural Missouri didn’t turn blue. Pemiscot moved more than any county in the state, and Fitzpatrick still carried it by 34 points. But the Republican advantage shrank almost everywhere, and higher turnout around Kansas City, St. Louis and Springfield magnified the shift.
Missouri Republicans suffer biggest electoral setback in a generation
A lot of ink has been spilled pouring over the results of an historic election in Missouri. Now comes the hard part for Democrats: turning a wave into power.
Republicans will hold 95 of 163 House seats in January. Democrats will hold 68. To take the chamber in 2028, Democrats need a net gain of 14.
There is a potential path. Fourteen Republican-held districts were decided by fewer than eight percentage points this year. Six are in St. Charles County, including Miller’s and two others Republicans held by 125 and 276 votes. The other eight are in St. Louis County and in Jackson, Jefferson, Boone and Jasper counties.
If Democrats gained another four percentage points of the two-party vote in every district, they would win 82 seats. That is a majority with nothing to spare.
It also assumes they lose nothing they won this year, and some of those wins are fragile. Suzanne Luther took her Jefferson City seat by 189 votes. And 2028 is a presidential year, with a bigger electorate. Republicans won every statewide race in the last two presidential elections by double digits.
The Senate offers Democrats fewer options. Republicans will hold a 22-12 majority. Three GOP seats on the 2028 ballot stand out: Joe Nicola’s in Jackson County, David Gregory’s in St. Louis County and Adam Schnelting’s in St. Charles County.
Nicola and Gregory each won in 2024 by fewer than five points, in a year Republicans carried the down-ballot statewide races by about 20. Schnelting won by about 10.

For some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again. But for others, crossing a finish line (of any distance) might feel like a natural point to take a break from the sport, or at least to significantly scale back.
Still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward. That way, you can go into a spring training cycle with a solid base.
Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, says Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.
Keeping a steady mileage base also allows you to experiment. “This gives you a chance to try new fuels, try new gear, a new pair of shorts, new pair of shoes, stuff you didn't like during your block,” Sheehy says. You could also experiment with pace. “This is a great block to think about moving your easy pace up 15 seconds to let your heart and body start adapting to that new norm.”
If you want to strike a balance between giving yourself a well-deserved break and completely reversing all of your gains, the question becomes: What’s the minimum running you can do to maintain your fitness? And how long can I do that without falling back?
Here’s what running coaches and an exercise physiologist have to say, plus what other forms of exercise come into play in the maintenance phase.

How Much Runners Can Reduce Mileage to Maintain Fitness
First, it’s important to note that taking a week or two off after a marathon and at least one week for the half is not only encouraged, it’s probably the best thing you can do for your body—and your mind.
“The thing I encourage all my runners to remember is patience,” says Sheehy. “Let your body heal and take that time.” He typically advises runners to take a full week off, then slowly add in easy miles without rushing to get back to quality workouts.
Then by the end of week two, you enter the true maintenance phase. “This is really an exciting time of running,” Sheehy says. “This is where we’re keeping 90 percent of the fitness with about 60 percent of the work.” He recommends taking the average mileage from your peak marathon training weeks rather than the single highest weekly mileage.
This tends to net out to between 20 and 30 miles a week in the maintenance phase for marathon runners and 10 to 15 miles a week for half-marathoners. That might look like three shorter, easier runs during the week and an 8- to 12-miler on the weekend. (Experts agree it’s best to run more frequently at lower volume for each run than do fewer, longer runs.) “That keeps you 90 percent fit, but allows you to enjoy running and not have the pressure of having to run six or five days a week and without having structured workouts,” Sheehy says.
Andrew M. Jones, Ph.D., professor of applied physiology at the University of Exeter in the U.K., puts the minimum effective dose of maintenance running slightly lower—at 50 percent—though after about four to six weeks at half the volume, runners will likely start to see “more significant deterioration,” he says, specifically of race-specific endurance. Most runners are familiar with the big muscles involved in running, such as the quads, hamstrings, and glutes. But there are lesser-known—yet still important—players that can influence running performance. One example: the quadratus lumborum, or QL for short.
A deep trunk muscle, the QL attaches to the lower spine and the back side of the pelvis, Nicole Haas, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and founder of Boulder Physiolab in Colorado, tells Runner’s World. It serves a few different functions in daily life, such as helping you arch your back, bend to the side, and rotate your upper body, Haas explains.
When you run, the QL plays more of a stabilizing role, working to control your pelvis and trunk while you stride, says Spencer Agnew, PT, DPT, a physical therapist at Sword Health and run coach with Wisconsin-based Ascent Endurance Group. The QL also assists with breathing, specifically when you inhale, Agnew adds.
If this muscle is tight or irritated, you’ll likely feel pain in your back or sacroiliac joints, which link the pelvis and lower spine, Agnew says. To help you avoid these aches, we asked the PTs to explain what can cause an angry QL and how to relieve it.
What Causes QL Pain?
There are several reasons your QL might be yelling at you. A common one? Your hip flexors are tight. In many cases, this yanks on your QL as well, because the psoas and QL both insert into the same group of vertebrae in your lower back, Agnew explains.
Another culprit is weak glutes. When your glutes aren’t strong enough to help you maintain good running mechanics, your knee can collapse inward as you land and your opposite-side hip can dip down, Haas explains. This, in turn, can cause your trunk to side bend and rotate, thus placing more strain on your QL over time. Running downhill can exacerbate the problem, Haas adds, because that can cause your lower back to arch and place further stress on your QL.

New Zealand’s central bank warned on Tuesday that global financial stability risks continue to rise, with growing vulnerabilities in the non-bank lending sector driven by increased private credit activity.
In its semi-annual Financial Stability Report, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) said non-bank lenders are becoming more active in the country, particularly in commercial property and development financing.
While greater competition offers benefits for borrowers, it creates risks that are harder for the RBNZ to monitor, as much of this activity falls outside the regulated sector, it said.
Read more: Private Credit and Stablecoins Pose Risks Beyond Size, BoE Governor Bailey Warns
“While systemic risks from non-bank lenders in New Zealand remain limited given their size, their growing role in credit provision highlights the importance of ongoing monitoring,” the report said.
Banks continue to account for the majority of lending to households and businesses in New Zealand, with direct finance and non-bank lending firms representing only about 6% of overall lending, official data showed. Private credit funds and non-bank lenders are not directly regulated by the RBNZ, which also serves as the country’s banking regulator.
The RBNZ highlighted how the recent failure of an Australian property developer exposed several private lenders to potential losses, with some funds restricting withdrawals amid increased redemption requests.
Last week, Australia’s corporate regulator said it would launch an official probe into the A$3.4 billion ($2.30 billion) collapse of Sydney homebuilder Bathla, putting fresh scrutiny on the fast-growing private credit sector, which has increasingly stepped in to finance developers as banks retreat from riskier lending.
The financial stability report also warned that heightened geopolitical tensions and financial market fragility had increased global risks, with Middle East tensions disrupting energy and trade flows.
However, the report said New Zealand’s financial system remained resilient.
“Domestic financial stress has generally eased from its peak last year but remains uneven,” RBNZ Governor Anna Breman said.
Despite some narrowing of lending margins, New Zealand’s banks are maintaining strong capital and liquidity positions, with recent stress tests showing banks and insurers could withstand severe financial shocks, Breman added.

[Editor’s Note: This Community Voices article was written by Daan Oxener, who is a Dutch entrepreneur and tennis player who somewhat accidentally found his way into Kapchorwa’s running culture. Since 2016, he has explored Mount Elgon’s many trails and everyday community life. Through Home of Friends Guesthouse and Run Kapchorwa, he helps adventurous travelers discover the people and stories behind Uganda’s Land of Champions.]
The moment you climb the tarmac road to Kapchorwa, Uganda, you are surrounded by rolling green hills, banana plantations, and small farms. There is little sign that you are approaching one of East Africa’s elite running hubs. Kapchorwa’s first impression is rural and rustic. No tartan running tracks or fancy facilities here.
Alvin, an ambitious U.K. runner with Ugandan roots, describes his first experience of running on Kapchorwa’s trails:
‘‘The trails are very scenic. You cross small villages and rivers. The trail surfaces are made of mud with small rocks, but they are quite smooth. You see a lot of farm life. You come across the locals, children walking to school. Nothing extravagant.’’
But in this unassuming environment, international athletes are pushing their limits. And so did Alvin.
‘‘Because of my excitement to find elite athletes, I pushed myself more than I should have. I was struggling to keep pace with a group of local runners. Later I was told that Jacob Kiplimo, the world half marathon and cross-country champion, was in this group.’’
Running in Kapchorwa is challenging and takes time to adapt to. We see this with almost every international runner who comes here for the first time. The rule, therefore, is simple: Change the altitude, but leave everything else the same.
Compared with the famous running hub of Iten, Kenya, its counterpart across the border, Kapchorwa is greener and hillier. The two places share ancestral Kalenjin roots, reflected in similarities in culture and food. In terms of infrastructure, however, they are quite different: Iten has more tarmac roads, and its running tourism infrastructure is more developed, with gyms and swimming pools catering to visiting athletes.
The Mount Elgon Rainforest
‘‘Give us the forest back, and we give Uganda more champions.’’
This recurring message from elders in the Mosopisiek community says a lot about the roots of Kapchorwa’s running culture.
In 1992, when the Ugandan portion of Mount Elgon National Park was officially gazetted, many Mosopisiek people were relocated from the rainforest to the lower flanks of the mountain.
This meant a big change in their way of life: from running for miles after stolen cows to settling in one area and growing potatoes or onions; from eating forest berries and mushrooms to eating grains and plantains.
But those roots have not disappeared. You can still experience them on trail runs and hikes through the stunning, undulating landscape.
Daily endurance, or “building stamina” as the natives often describe it, starts from a young age. Children walk kilometers to school. In their free time, they jump over steep rocks and mountain streams.
The terrain itself is a training ground.

Today’s big story: Could Nvidia Stock Fall 50%? Follow The Cash
Apple (AAPL) stock trades at 36.0 times its earnings over the last twelve months, counted as normalized net income plus stock-based pay after tax, with the shares near their highest close of the past year. That is a high price for one year of profit, so it is worth setting against the profit expected over the next two fiscal years. So what sales and profit does that price assume Apple will deliver?
Apple Investors Bet On Higher Sales At Thinner Margins
The consensus forecast projects Apple’s revenue will reach $528 billion in fiscal 2027, compared with the $479 billion reported for fiscal 2026. Forecasted net income rises far less, moving to $135 billion from $132 billion. Those figures leave a net margin of 25.6% in fiscal 2027, below the 27.6% Apple reported for fiscal 2026.
For fiscal 2028, the forecast models a 7.4% increase in revenue and a 10.3% rise in net income. That puts the net margin at 26.3%, still short of fiscal 2026. The bet is on more sales, not on more profit from each dollar of sales.
On that forecast, you pay 38.0 times the average analyst estimate of Apple’s net income for fiscal 2027. That is not measured the same way as the 36.0 times trailing figure, which adds stock-based pay after tax to normalized net income. On fiscal 2028 earnings the price is 34.4 times, though that year’s forecast is uncertain: the gap between the highest and lowest per-share estimates is 23.8% of the average.
How Fast Has Apple Actually Been Growing?
Apple’s latest year ran faster than the forecast: revenue increased 15.1% in fiscal 2026, after 6.4% growth in fiscal 2025. The consensus forecast for fiscal 2027 works out to about 10% growth. Neither forecasted margin surpasses what the company has already reached: Apple reported a net margin of 26.9% in fiscal 2025 and posted a higher margin in fiscal 2026.
The iPhone led that growth, with sales rising 21.2% in fiscal 2026. Services, Apple’s second-largest business, grew 13.0%.
Management guidance points to a slower start for fiscal 2027. Apple expects December quarter revenue to grow 7% to 10%. Management said this range reflects constrained supply, noting that revenue grew 16% in the same quarter a year before. The company also expects a gross margin of 45% to 46%. Management said most of the margin decline from the September quarter comes from higher memory costs.
Where Could Apple Fall Short Of The Forecast?
Supply is the first place. Management expects memory to constrain the Mac and iPad in the December quarter because demand has been higher than it expected. Apple provides no outlook beyond that quarter. If those constraints last, the fiscal 2027 sales forecast could come down.
The cost of memory is the other place. Beyond the December quarter, management sees memory prices still rising and expects less help over time from memory already in inventory. Price increases on the Mac, iPad and iPhone have offset some of that impact, but further cost rises could push Apple’s net margin below the forecast.
If the forecast holds, the forward multiples are a fair picture of Apple’s price. Supply is where the forecast is most likely to fall short, and lower sales alongside rising memory costs would leave the stock priced for profit Apple may never earn, a riskier bet. During a marathon, Juli Windsor admits she doesn’t always get to take in the scenery.
“Most runners can see what's coming ahead, and they can see beyond the shoulders and all the heads,” she said. “For me, my view is hundreds of butts. It’s not the most inspirational view.”
It’s one difference that Windsor, who is 3-foot-9, has learned to navigate as a runner with dwarfism. But that hasn't stopped her from beating many of those butts in races.
At the Indianapolis Marathon on November 7, Windsor, 39, ran 3:42:00 to finish in the top third of her 35–39 age group, averaging an 8:28 mile pace. The time was a PR by seven minutes and is provisionally a new American record for the T40 para category (a division for athletes with short stature).
Windsor was born with an extremely rare form of dwarfism called acromesomelic dysplasia. “Last I heard, I’m one of a million,” said Windsor, who works as a physician assistant in developmental pediatrics.
Windsor’s run in Indianapolis is more impressive considering that this is part two of her marathoning career. After taking a decade off to raise her two kids in 2014, Windsor has come back even stronger, knocking off more than an hour from her pre-hiatus personal best.
“I just think the human body is just such an amazing thing,” she said. “And that when asked something difficult of it, what you’re capable of doing can sometimes be really surprising.”
Finding her stride
As a middle schooler, Windsor joined the track team to hang out with her friends and went in with low expectations. But that changed when she beat another runner in an 800-meter race. It was motivating, and Windsor eventually realized that although she couldn’t dust her peers in a sprint, she had exceptional grit and endurance. “I might not be able to outrun them, but I could outlast them,” she remembers.
In her twenties, Windsor set her sights on the marathon—and one marathon in particular. She wanted to become the first person with dwarfism to run the prestigious Boston Marathon. In 2013, her dream almost came true, but as she neared the finish line on Boylston Street, she was forced to stop. Terrorists had detonated bombs at the finish. Windsor was unharmed, but her dream would have to wait.
The next year, Windsor became the first person with dwarfism to complete the historic race, running 4:43:26. That would be her last marathon for a decade, as Windsor raised two kids and focused on her family.

Not long after, Windsor started working with coach Esther Atkins, a former professional marathoner who coaches with McKirdy Trained. The first time I entered the New York City Marathon drawing, I got in. I’m not sure what possessed me that day to apply, having never run another race in my life. I figured I’d never get in, so why not? I played soccer growing up, and when the world shut down during COVID-19, running became the easiest way to get out of the house and see my friends. That’s where my running journey began.
My NYC Marathon training also happened during my senior year of college, which brought its own challenges. While I was excited to run, I also didn’t want to miss out on any of the socializing that happened that year. I did my best to make it to every party, every club soccer game, and anything in between while running as much as possible. I was scared that running was going to infringe on my everyday life and I wouldn’t have time to keep having fun. Despite all of that, I had caught the marathon bug and after finishing the New York City Marathon in 2022, I went on to run the Paris and Chicago Marathons in 2024.
Training Without a Plan
While training for those first few marathons, I didn’t have any real plan, except to not let it interfere with my social calendar. My strategy consisted of building up mileage in order to reach 20 miles about four weeks out from race day. In between, I pieced together training information from influencers on Instagram and Google searches (this was pre-ChatGPT!). Now that I’m a Runner’s World+ member, I have all those resources right at my fingertips.
Although I caught the marathon bug almost instantly, I also felt defeated after New York. I knew I could have done better. Between New York City in 2022 and Paris in 2024, I never ran more than 10 miles at a time, but I was running enough that I knew I could do it again if I really wanted. I followed a similar approach for Chicago in 2024: Build up to one long run about a month out, then fill the rest of the weeks with shorter runs and one medium-length run. It wasn’t much of a plan, but it worked for me. My times kept improving, and I broke four hours for the first time in Chicago.
Looking back, I realize that my no-plan approach was partly a way to protect myself. If I never said my goal out loud, I couldn’t feel disappointed if I missed it. Breaking four hours in Chicago changed that. For the first time, I wanted to see what I could do with a real plan.

I wanted to beat my time in Chicago and get as close to 3 hours and 45 minutes as possible.

JPMorgan Chase (JPM) said Tuesday that longtime CFO Jeremy Barnum will step down next year in the latest change among the top ranks of the country's largest bank as it prepares for CEO Jamie Dimon's eventual succession.
Barnum, who has served as the bank's CFO since 2021, will be succeeded by Bregje de Best, CFO of JPMorgan's commercial and investment bank, after the company's first quarter earnings in April, according to a JPMorgan filing.
Barnum will become vice chair, remaining with the bank until early 2028, JPMorgan said. Dimon added in a press release statement that Barnum had requested the transition after six years in the role.
That tenure is slightly above average for a CFO at a large US company, according to a 2025 study by executive search firm Spencer Stuart, which found CFOs at S&P 500 companies had served an average of 4.8 years in their positions.
The announcement comes less than a week after Allison Beer, JPMorgan's head of credit card and connected commerce, informed colleagues that she was leaving to pursue another opportunity, according to an internal JPMorgan memo.
It also follows a broader leadership shake-up of Dimon's top lieutenants earlier this year when JPMorgan announced the retirement of Marianne Lake, the former head of its sprawling consumer bank and previously a leading candidate to succeed Dimon.
The announcement of Lake's departure also came as JPMorgan said it was elevating executives Doug Petno and Troy Rohrbaugh to the role of co-president, signaling their leads to eventually take the reins from Dimon, who was expected to stay for three more years as CEO, according to an executive familiar with the matter who spoke to Yahoo Finance at the time.
Barnum's planned transition and Lake's retirement are part of a broader effort to prepare JPMorgan's next generation of leadership, according to a person familiar with the bank's succession planning.
The person characterized Beer's departure as separate, saying the credit card executive was seeking a broader leadership role than her current responsibilities at the bank.
De Best, 43, joined JPMorgan in 2006 and has held senior positions across investment banking, markets and corporate banking. She will also join the firm's operating committee when she assumes the CFO role.
Morgan Stanley analyst Manan Gosalia said Tuesday his team "do[es] not expect the CFO transition itself to have any impact on JPM's strategy or preliminary 2027 outlook."
RBC Capital Markets analyst Gerard Cassidy also told clients Tuesday, in reaction to Barnum's departure, that senior management shake-ups are not unusual at JPMorgan.
"We expect JPM's deep management bench will continue to enable the company to effectively manage through senior executive realignment," Cassidy said.

Charlie Bilello Calls Leveraged Single-Stock ETFs ‘One of the Worst Financial Innovations’
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Charlie Bilello went after one of Wall Street’s fastest-growing product lines on November 16, 2026. In a post on X, Bilello wrote: “One of the worst financial innovations: Leveraged and inverse single-stock ETFs. -38% median investor return. >$500 million in management fees collected.”
Bilello was quoting Peter Mallouk, who pointed out that investors can now choose from 600+ ETFs linked to a single stock. Many of them add leverage, and their median expense ratio is 1% a year. Mallouk’s point was that ETFs won investors over by offering diversification and low fees. These funds put all the risk on one stock and charge more for it.
How Daily Resets Quietly Eat Returns
A leveraged single-stock ETF tries to deliver a multiple, usually 2x, of one stock’s move for a single day. An inverse fund tries to deliver the opposite of that move. The word that matters is daily. These funds reset their exposure every session, so over weeks or months their returns drift away from a simple multiple of what the stock did.
Here’s a simple example. Say a stock rises 10% one day and falls 10% the next. The stock ends down 1%. A 2x fund gains 20% and then loses 20%, which leaves it down 4%. This drag is called volatility decay. It gets worse as the stock gets choppier, and the funds tend to track the most volatile names in the market.
Fees make it worse. The GraniteShares 2x Long NVDA Daily ETF (NASDAQ:NVDL) has a net expense ratio of 1.64%[1], according to its prospectus. Then there is investor behavior. Traders tend to pile in after a big run and bail out after a sharp drop, locking in losses at the worst moments. That pattern helps explain why Charlie Bilello puts the median investor return at -38%. Over the same period, Charlie Bilello says the funds collected more than $500 million in management fees.
Why Leveraged Funds Clash With Retirement Goals
Income investors need two things: capital that compounds and cash that keeps coming. Leveraged single-stock funds work against both. They pay little or no real income, they experience decay, and a deep drop takes years of normal returns to recover. These funds are built as day-trading tools, a poor match for most retirement goals.

Having your first marathon result erased after months of training might be enough to send anyone into a downward spiral. Andrea Sager, though, has been getting some serious mileage out of the bad news on Instagram.
"Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.
The Houston attorney and mother of two found out she was DQ’d days after the November 1 race when footage surfaced of her smoking marijuana on the course. The moment she decided to accept a puff from a spectator was caught on video, and New York Road Runners subsequently removed her finish time from its records.
As far as the rules go, there's little room for debate. NYRR's Code of Conduct explicitly prohibits "smoking, vaping, or use of electronic smoking devices, tobacco products, or marijuana products" in the starting corrals, on the course, and in the finish area, with the restriction extending 1,000 feet beyond those locations.
In a video explaining her disqualification, Sager acknowledged breaking the rules and said she understood the decision. Even so, she claimed she wasn’t the only runner to drink alcohol or smoke weed during the race, and suggested the difference was having the moment seen by millions of people on social media.
"I wasn't planning on smoking weed on the course, but I was in so much pain and needed something to help me finish," she told the New York Post.
Sager hasn't let the penalty spoil her memories of race day. Her original finish-line recap described a grueling 26.2 miles that involved "approximately 47 mental breakdowns," although she was thrilled to check the race off her bucket list. She later reminded followers that the experience could not be taken away from her.
She'd been having plenty of fun long before arriving in New York, too. One prerace Instagram video joked about giving up dating apps in favor of training for a marathon, while her bright pink marathon shirt doubled as a personal advertisement. The front read, "Andrea, 35, Single. Great Credit. Bad Judgment," while the back added, "Looking for a man with more endurance than my ex."
Her latest social media introduction has since acquired another word: "35. Single. Great credit. Poor judgment. Disqualified."
Sager still has her finisher medal, and the extra attention has brought some unexpected opportunities.
"I'm talking with the brands now, so there's a lot of upside, but still annoying," she told the Post.
Sager said she was told she can participate in future NYRR events, despite the removal of her November 1 result. Runner's World contacted the organization for comment and confirmation of her eligibility but received no response.
As for racing plans, Sager said she has HYROX Houston on her calendar for April 2027. And someone in her Instagram comments has suggested a shirt idea for her next event:
"I smoked weed at the NYC marathon and all I got was a DQ."

US Senate seeks to restore campaign finance watchdog during lame-duck session
Voters mark their ballots on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at the University of Alaska, Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)
The U.S. Senate took a first step Tuesday toward reviving the moribund Federal Election Commission, holding a confirmation hearing on President Donald Trump’s nominees to lead the campaign finance watchdog after it was sidelined for the midterm elections.
The FEC has lacked a quorum for more than a year, preventing it from taking action on complaints or issuing advisory opinions. As its backlog of work has grown, candidates and political groups have been left uncertain about when — or if — the FEC will take action on alleged violations of federal campaign finance law.
The Senate Rules and Administration Committee on Tuesday weighed the nominations of two Republicans, Ashley Stow and Andrew Woodson, to join the FEC. Only two commissioners, both Democrats, are currently serving and the agency needs a bipartisan quorum of at least four to take official action.
“Restoring the commission’s ability to function is especially important following the 2026 midterm elections,” said Sen. Bill Hagerty, a Tennessee Republican who chaired the hearing.
Hagerty pointed to the backlog of complaints and the need to prepare for the 2028 presidential race. Restoring a quorum will allow the FEC “to resume its essential responsibilities,” he said.
The FEC enforces federal campaign finance laws and assists candidates and donors in complying with them. The FEC, which marked its 50th anniversary in 2025, also makes public a vast trove of campaign finance data.
The hearing marked an effort by Republicans to end the FEC’s dormancy during the Senate’s lame-duck period before Democrats take control of the chamber in January. At that point, Democrats will have much more power to demand that the White House nominate individuals acceptable to Democrats or block Trump’s nominees.
Democrats support restoring a quorum on the FEC, but they question whether Trump will allow commissioners to act independently.
In February 2025, Trump fired the Democratic chair of the FEC, Ellen Weintraub, who had been a commissioner since 2002. Weintraub has said she doesn’t view the firing as legally valid, though she hasn’t challenged the dismissal in court.
The move against Weintraub came after Republican Sean Cooksey resigned before Trump’s inauguration. In April 2025, Republican Allen Dickerson also resigned, creating a lack of a quorum that has persisted.
Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said Tuesday the FEC was established in the post-Watergate era to be evenly balanced between Democrats and Republicans and politically independent. Padilla is the ranking Democrat on the committee but will likely chair the panel beginning in January.
“It’s absolutely critical that any commissioners who sign on to help lead this agency commit to restoring and defending that independence. Full stop,” Padilla said.
The Trump administration has broadly sought to bring independent agencies created by Congress under the control of the White House. The U.S. Supreme Court in June allowed the president to fire members of the Federal Trade Commission without cause. It’s not clear how that decision would apply to firings of members of the FEC.

“Some runs are shouts, and some runs are whispers,” I wrote a few decades back in Runner’s World Complete Book of Women’s Running, an attempt to capture the many moods—the many functions—that running served in my life. I scrolled past the phrase recently on social media: Somebody had designed it with colors and typography and posted it, apparently finding resonance in the sentiment.
I chuckled a little upon seeing it. If I wrote that today, I’d add something else: “Some runs are walks.”
This new reality that came with illness and settled in for the long haul wasn’t easy to accept. I’ve been running on and off for more than 50 years, some 85 percent of my life. I jogged along with my older brother when I was a girl, competed in high school as a teen, trained for a sub-3 marathon as a working professional in my 30s, plodded with a baby jogger in my 40s. Now, past 60, running has shape-shifted again. The transformation is different this time, the lessons deeper and, frankly, a little harder to grasp. But after a period of struggle, I’ve made peace with it. Because as usual, if you dare to listen, running will speak to you.
Most of us who run spend years or even decades seeking to improve, from a 5K to 10K, from breaking 4 hours in a marathon to then trying for 3:45. For a long time, wherever you are, improvement is possible, and change generally trends in one direction. Not every run, of course. The body has good days and challenging ones; that variability is a given, and progress is not a straight line. But we can expect a trajectory that provides a satisfactory feedback loop, one of betterment.
Inevitably, aging will bend the line of progression into an arc. We can know that and still have trouble seeing it at first, because the heavy legs or knee catching feels like just another hard day. Nothing a little rest or cross-training can’t solve.
If seeing it is difficult, accepting it can be even harder. The forward march has been the natural state of things for so long. The battle waged for incremental increases in mileage or decreases in time was never easy. Shouldn’t I be pushing past this? Isn’t it what runners do?
Running taught me to be tough. For years, that served me even beyond the sport. In work, the tug of fatigue from long nights at the ad agency felt familiar and manageable as a long run. Giving birth called back the discipline of breathing through pain; the years of motherhood to come called in the lessons of patience, of quietly putting in the hours without immediate affirmation or result. I loved being a badass in the endurance sport of life. The ability to override tiredness felt powerful. I enjoyed telling myself I was fine when evidence pointed to the contrary. I relished pushing against edges and limits.
Until the day I woke, swung my feet over the side of the bed to stand, and felt the world spin wildly out of control. The floor rushed up to my face, and I curled in a ball seeking safety and stillness. Confusion mingled with nausea. I could feel the whirling even with eyes closed. The fetal position proved fitting. I’d spend years relearning how to be in this new world, where vertigo could strike at any time.
My first reaction was “I’ll fight!” Though for months that thought came while I was sprawled on the couch, unable to focus my eyes or lift my arms.
